Operation Barbarossa. Operation Barbarossa was Nazi Germany's massive invasion of the Soviet Union beginning in June 1941. It was the largest military campaign in history by scale and casualties. Adolf Hitler launched the offensive to conquer living space, called Lebensraum, for the German people and to destroy communism. Over three million German troops and allies attacked across a vast front. The Soviets absorbed catastrophic early losses but eventually stabilized their defenses and counterattacked, inflicting decisive defeats on German forces at Stalingrad and Kursk. Barbarossa shaped the entire Eastern Front's character as a brutal, ideological war of annihilation that claimed over twenty-seven million lives and determined that the Soviet Union, not Germany, would dominate Eastern Europe after 1945.

Hitler's 1939 Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, the Nazi-Soviet Non-Aggression Pact, was always meant as temporary. Hitler believed Germany needed the Soviet Union's territory and resources, and the Nazis and Communists were ideological enemies. German planners expected to destroy the Soviet Army and conquer Moscow, Leningrad, and the oil fields of the Caucasus within months using the Blitzkrieg formula. Germany amassed three point two million troops including Germans, Romanians, Hungarians, Finns, and Italians, along with thirty-six hundred tanks and twenty-seven hundred aircraft.

Barbarossa began on June 22, 1941, with a dawn assault on a sixteen hundred mile front. German armies advanced rapidly, enveloping vast numbers of Soviet troops. By October 1941, German forces besieged Leningrad in a nine hundred day siege that killed one million civilians and nearly reached Moscow. Soviet counteroffensives in December 1941 halted German advances near Moscow. The myth of Blitzkrieg invincibility was shattered as Germany faced a long war it could not sustain.

German forces regrouped and attacked southward toward the oil fields and the city of Stalingrad on the Volga River. The Battle of Stalingrad from August 1942 to February 1943 became the turning point when the Sixth Army was encircled and destroyed, ending German offensive capacity in the East. Soviet counteroffensives pushed German forces westward, and Germany would never again mount a strategic offensive on the Eastern Front.

Barbarossa killed approximately twenty-seven million Soviets, military and civilian, making it the war's deadliest theater. The German genocide of Soviet Jews as part of the Holocaust and the systematic murder of Soviet prisoners of war with three million dying in captivity made Barbarossa an ideological war of annihilation. Soviet victory at Stalingrad and Kursk secured Soviet domination of Eastern Europe and set the stage for Soviet armies to reach Berlin in 1945.
